plain: Several challenges slow solar panel adoption despite falling costs. Upfront installation cost remains a major barrier for many homeowners, even though panels pay for themselves over time, since financing isn't accessible to everyone. Intermittency is a real technical challenge, since solar only generates during daylight, requiring either grid backup or expensive battery storage to be reliable around the clock. Grid infrastructure in many regions wasn't designed for distributed generation, requiring costly upgrades to handle two-way power flow from homes back into the grid. Space constraints limit adoption for renters, apartment dwellers, or homes with heavily shaded or poorly oriented roofs. Permitting and installation processes can be slow and bureaucratic, varying significantly by location. Finally, policy inconsistency, such as changing subsidies or net metering rules, creates uncertainty that discourages both consumers and installers from committing long-term.

plain: Futures and options are both derivative contracts, but they differ in obligation and risk. An options contract gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (a call) or sell (a put) an asset at a set price before expiration, meaning the buyer's maximum loss is limited to the premium paid, while the seller takes on greater risk if exercised. Because of this asymmetry, options require paying an upfront premium for that flexibility, while futures typically don't, only margin deposits.
